cultivar: Yunnan large-leaf (assamica) populations, often old-tree or wild-arbor material
processing: Withered, rolled and oxidised like a black tea, but dried in the sun (sometimes finished at low heat) instead of being baked at high temperature, so the leaf keeps a little enzyme activity and can change with storage.
harvest_season: Spring (March–April) for the best lots; autumn shai hong is common and softer.
appearance_dry: Large, loosely twisted leaves in dark red-brown rather than black, duller than baked Dian Hong, with brownish-gold tips.
appearance_liquor: Amber to orange-red, a shade lighter than baked black tea, clear and thick.
appearance_wet: Big, pliable red-brown leaves, often with a greenish tint at the stem in young tea.
taste_profile: Plum, dried apricot and honey with a faint sun-dried-hay freshness and sometimes a trace of tartness when young; rounder and more raisin-like after a couple of years.

brewing.notes: Use water near the boil; it has a sheng-like structure and goes flat with cool water. Pressed cakes need a 10-second rinse first. Good brewed grandpa-style in a big mug too.

vintage_note: The one Yunnan black that is sold by vintage: shops list the pressing or picking year, and lots from roughly 2015 to the current spring are on the market, loose or pressed into 100–357 g cakes and dragon balls. Young (0–1 year) it can show a green or sour edge; 2–5 years is where most people like it, and makers claim it keeps improving for a decade.
description:
Shai hong is Yunnan black tea finished in the sun. Instead of baking the oxidised leaf dry at high temperature, the way every other black tea is made, farmers spread it out to dry under the sun the way they dry pu-erh maocha. Yunnan villagers made it like this for home use long before it had a market name; around 2013–2015 it became a product in its own right, and now most Yunnan black-tea makers offer one.

The low drying temperature is the whole point. It leaves a little enzyme activity in the leaf, so the tea is not 'finished' when it is packed: it keeps changing, and it can be stored and aged like a pu-erh cake rather than drunk fast like a Dian Hong. It also means the sweet-potato and caramel notes that baking creates never fully form, which is why shai hong tastes fruitier and brighter than baked Yunnan black.

Young, it is plum and dried apricot with honey, a hay-like freshness and sometimes a faint sourness that puts some people off. Give a cake two or three years and the sour edge goes, the fruit turns to raisin and the texture thickens. Brew it with water near the boil in a gaiwan or just steep it loose in a big mug; cool water makes it taste thin. Expect eight or more steeps from good material.

It is sold by year, loose or pressed into small cakes and dragon balls, often from old-tree or 'wild' arbor leaf in Lincang, Pu'er and Baoshan. Because the market is young there is no grading system; buy from makers who state the year, the area and whether the leaf is plantation or arbor, and taste before buying several years' worth. Lots that smell musty or vinegary were stored badly, not aged well.

It pairs naturally with a pu-erh habit: if you already keep cakes, a couple of shai hong bings in the same box cost little and give you something to compare against your sheng as the years pass.
sources_note: Commercial emergence dated to roughly 2013–2015 from vendor and trade accounts; no formal origin year exists. Ageing claims beyond ~5 years are maker claims.
